quote: Forage is very scarce, and we have mainly to rely on grass for the animals
says: Lee to President Davis, 23 June (before the army crossed the Potomac): forage was very scarce and the army had mainly to rely on grass for its animals.
feature: grass and forage for the army's animals, late June

about.region: the districts of the Potomac and the Cumberland Valley the army marched through

note: A letter of the commanding general (headed 'Headquarters Army of Northern Virginia, June 23, 1863'), not a description of any field: it says the army's animals lived on grass (grazed or cut) in the districts it passed, which is the reason a meadow or pasture near the line of march may stand short or cut in the days that follow. No field of the theatre is named.

quote: grass and grain sliould be cut and fed to the animals ; if tliey are turned into the fields, thfjy destroy more than they consun:e
says: Lee to Pickett, 9 July at Hagerstown: the grass and grain should be cut and fed to the animals; if they are turned into the fields they destroy more than they consume (the OCR prints 'sliould', 'tliey', 'thfjy' and 'consun:e').
feature: grass and grain cut as fodder, Maryland, 9 July

about.region: the Hagerstown and Williamsport district of Maryland

note: An instruction of the commanding general about how the animals of one division are to be fed in Maryland on 9 July: grass and grain cut and carried, not grazed. It dates the practice in the window of the schedule; it names no field.

quote: Some of the wheat was fed to horses, which would otherwise have been without feed
says: Prince, the night of 9 to 10 July at the Boonsborough and Williamsport turnpike (Maryland): some of the wheat of the field in which his division bivouacked was fed to horses that would otherwise have been without feed.
feature: wheat cut and stacked, fed to horses, Washington County, Maryland

about.region: Washington County, Maryland, about 35 miles south-west

note: The same report as VC-OR-020 (the wheat of that field was already cut and in stacks, which the men slept on): the stacked wheat was also used to feed horses. The field is not near Gettysburg; it dates a use of cut wheat in the same agricultural region and season.

quote: Besides destroying tbe wheat aad oats, •bicb they used for bedding, the bluecoats bad burned his rails
says: The study of the Eisenhower farm's history reports Philip Redding's damage claim: Union troops camped in his oat and wheat fields on the night of 1 July, their horses were pastured in his meadows, and they used the wheat and oats they destroyed for bedding and burned his rails.
feature: the Redding farm on Willoughby Run: oat and wheat fields camped on, meadows grazed
note: The study's account of a claimant's sworn statement (the claim lists 10 acres of wheat, 20 of oats and 40 of grass); the same passage dates a cavalry raid to 10 July by a regiment the study itself says was not at Gettysburg, so the claim's dates are the claimant's, not the study's. The text layer of this typescript is badly damaged (letters read as other letters): the quote is kept as saved. The farm is not one of the farmsteads of the structures layer, so the claim is not placed.
